source.title: Revisiting End-To-End Sparse Autoencoder Training: A Short Finetune Is All You Need

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether changing SAE training objectives and fine-tuning changes reconstruction-induced cross-entropy loss, bearing on the training-artifact version of the claim. It does not test the original claim’s error decomposition or tokenwise scaling measurements.
record.gate_note: The reported cross-entropy comparisons after SAE training or fine-tuning bear on V6. SAEBench scores, adapter comparisons, and weight-stability plots do not directly measure the versions’ specified dark-matter properties and are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports how far changing the SAE training objective (KL+MSE fine-tuning or end-to-end training) shrinks the cross-entropy gap caused by SAE reconstruction error. That bears on V6's claim that dark matter shrinks with end-to-end-style training. The headline result, a 20–50% gap reduction against MSE-only SAEs, is stated in the abstract but not captured by any row. The recorded rows compare the study's own fine-tune against full E2E training instead.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The author concludes that a short KL+MSE fine-tune at the end of SAE training reduces the CE loss gap by 20–50%. This matches or beats full E2E training at much lower cost. Several fine-tuning methods give similar, non-additive gains, suggesting an easily correctable error source in MSE-trained SAEs. SAEBench results are mixed and depend on architecture and metric.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares MSE-only SAE training, short KL+MSE fine-tuning, and full end-to-end KL+MSE training using reconstruction-induced cross-entropy loss. It does not perform the original study’s analysis of linear predictability, per-token error norms, or token overlap across SAE sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported fine-tuning comparison varies with SAE sparsity: K=20 shows worse performance and incomplete convergence, while K=40, 80, and 160 match or exceed full end-to-end training. The author also notes that results may depend on training data and learning-rate tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: LoRA, linear and MLP adapters and KL fine-tuning each reduce the CE gap, but their gains do not stack. A rank-2 LoRA on the SAE captures over half of the fine-tune gain, and linear or MLP adapters capture about 60%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The objective-dependent part of MSE-trained SAE error is a common, low-rank, easily correctable component.

fits_no_version.finding: E2E SAEs reach similar CE loss to fine-tuned SAEs but score worse on RAVEL, absorption, TPP and SCR. KL fine-tuning gives mixed SAEBench changes that depend on architecture.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reducing reconstruction-induced loss through KL training trades off against downstream interpretability metrics.

record.problems: The cross-entropy comparisons are presented in figures without extractable numeric values or reported uncertainty. The study does not compare reconstruction errors to random errors of matched size and does not directly measure dark-matter structure or establish what fraction of it is attributable to training.
record.rows_left_out: No directly relevant result rows were omitted. SAEBench downstream metrics, adapter ablations, and weight-stability analyses were left out because they do not directly measure the claim versions’ specified properties.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of the SAE error vector from the input activation.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, overlap of failing contexts, and persistence with scale.
Comparison of reconstruction-induced loss against random errors of matched norm.
Separation of linear and nonlinear error components, and their relation to unlearned or dictionary-resistant features.
Circuit or steering analyses with versus without the error term; the authors only speculate about error nodes.
Error norm or fraction of variance unexplained after KL training; isolation of sparsity penalty, shrinkage, or dead latents as causes; architecture comparisons on dark matter.

missing.what: CE loss gap of MSE-only SAEs vs. the same SAEs after KL+MSE fine-tuning, with a 20–50% reduction stated.
At K=160, MSE-only training gives CE results comparable to or slightly better than KL+MSE E2E training.
Adapter and LoRA-on-SAE CE reductions and their non-additivity.
missing.locator: Section 4.1; Appendix C Figure 6; Appendix D Figure 7

record.verdict_notes: The study's results are figure-only, with no uncertainty reported. The CE gap measures the functional cost of the SAE error, not the error vector itself, so the V6 bearing is indirect. The existing rows R1–R5 benchmark the study's method against E2E training and should be replaced by MSE-only vs. KL-trained comparisons.

versions.untested_parts: Whether SAE error is a large linear function of the input activation.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, overlap in contexts where larger and smaller SAEs fail, and whether error persists with scale.
No comparison against random errors of the same size.
No separation of predictable and nonlinear error components, or test of whether either component corresponds to unlearned or dictionary-resistant features.
No circuit or steering analysis comparing results with and without an SAE error term.

The study tests effects of training objectives and fine-tuning on reconstruction-induced cross-entropy loss. It does not establish that most dark matter is a training artifact, isolate sparsity penalties, shrinkage, or dead latents as causes, or test whether a better SAE architecture removes it.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M
rows.operation_detail: Compared KL+MSE fine-tuning on the final 25M tokens with full end-to-end KL+MSE training.
rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss gap from SAE reconstructions
rows.note: The caption says the short fine-tuning approach performs slightly better than full end-to-end training on the same amount of data.
rows.check: This compares the study's own method (KL+MSE fine-tune) against another KL-based method (full E2E) on Pythia-160M. Both arms use the KL objective, so the row cannot show whether objective choice shrinks dark matter. It is a method-vs-method comparison, not a V6 measurement.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared KL+MSE fine-tuning on the final 25M tokens with MSE-only training.
rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss gap from SAE reconstructions
rows.note: The text reports that at K=20 the fine-tuning approach performs worse and shows incomplete convergence; it suggests more data or learning-rate tuning may be needed.
rows.check: The baseline is wrong: Figure 2 compares the KL+MSE fine-tune with full E2E training, not with MSE-only training. The row compares the study's own method with another method. Worse convergence at K=20 concerns the fine-tune recipe, not dark matter.

relationships.condition: Gemma-2-2B and Pythia-160M, TopK and ReLU SAEs, MSE-only training vs. a 25M-token KL+MSE fine-tune
relationships.reason: Per the text (abstract, Sec 4.1), not the rows: KL+MSE fine-tuning cuts the CE gap only 20–50%. At K=160, MSE-only roughly matches E2E, so most of the harmful error remains. Rows to be added (see missing).
relationships.display_finding: KL+MSE fine-tuning reduced the cross-entropy gap by 20–50%, with ReLU/TopK SAEBench runs using 15M tokens separately from the 25M-token comparisons; at K=160 on Gemma-2-2B, MSE-only training roughly matched end-to-end training, while KL+MSE fine-tuning still helped.

relation.reason: The study measures how changing SAE training objectives changes reconstruction-induced CE loss.

tranche.reason: The objective comparisons bear on qualifications to V6 by measuring incomplete reductions in reconstruction-induced downstream harm.

source_check.notes: CE-gap reduction measures functional fidelity, not the fraction of activation error removed or its representational origin. The pack supplies no rows to check.

statements.correction: Abstract: CE-gap reduction 20–50%. Section 4.1: Gemma-2-2B, 65K width, K=160, MSE-only comparable to or slightly better than full E2E; KL+MSE fine-tuning still beneficial. Appendix A.1: final 25M-token fine-tune; Pythia-160M tested at K=80, width 16K. Section 4.2 and Appendix A.2: ReLU and TopK SAEBench fine-tuning used 15M tokens.
statements.problem: The conditions conflate the 25M-token comparisons with the ReLU SAEBench experiments, which used 15M tokens. The K=160 result is specific to Gemma-2-2B.
